newsitem.title: USA: U.S. home sales jump, seen remaining strong in '97.
newsitem.headline: U.S. home sales jump, seen remaining strong in '97.

text.p: Americans' confidence in the economy continued to shine through in May, evidenced by the strongest level in existing home sales in a year.
"We are seeing a housing market which is roaring along," said John Tuccillo, economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR).
The NAR on Wednesday reported that sales of existing homes rose 4.4 percent in May to a 4.24 million annual unit rate, well above Wall Street economists' forecasts for a 4.07 million rate.
Sales had slipped 2.4 percent to a 4.06 million rate in April.

"At this point, with five months of data in, it looks pretty good we will have a four-million plus year, which would make it one of the top three years on record, depending on how much above four million we break," Tuccillo said.
But, he put the odds of another monthly increase in June at about 30 percent.
Tuccillo expressed surprise at the rebound in activity in May, adding, "I guess you can't underestimate the value of (strong) consumer confidence and employment."
Sales jumped in all regions of the country except the Northeast, an area that showed only a marginal decline in sales.
The largest increase was in the south, with sales rising to a 1.58 million rate in May from 1.46 million in April.
The Midwest also posted a large gain, jumping to a 1.07 million rate from 1.01 million. Economists attributed much of the increase in the midwest to a rebound after the floods earlier in the year.
The 4.24 million rate marks the highest since the 4.28 million pace seen in May 1996.
"People are confident to start stepping out and willing to commit to a mortgage," said John Ryding, senior economist at Bear, Stearns & Co Inc.

He said the May numbers reflected activity from a few months ago since sales tend to lag. And, with long-term interest rates having fallen significantly in the past few months, he noted, "We should see further strength."

The benchmark 30-year bond yielded 6.71 percent on Wednesday morning, down more than a 1/4-point from just a month ago. Similarly, the 10-year note, which is often linked to mortgage rates, yielded 6.42 percent, down from a high of 6.79 percent in late May and nearly 7.0 percent in mid-April.
Along with the expected housing strength, economists said it was a good bet that consumer spending should pick up as homeowners need to furnish their homes.
Analysts, though, were perplexed by the housing market strength, noting that the market should not be this strong more than six years into the latest economic expansion.
As such, Merrill Lynch & Co Inc senior economist Cheryl Katz said home sales should rise a bit more before levelling off.
"After several years of robust housing activity, pent-up demand for home sales has been largely exhausted," she said.
The NAR's Tuccillo agreed sales numbers should diminish somewhat later in 1997.
As for now, he said, it was clear the surge in the stock market, which has created an abundance in wealth, along with increased job security and solid job growth, will keep the housing market strong.

Indeed, the median home price jumped 4.8 percent in May to $123,200 from $117,600 in May 1996 and $120,700 in April. The price increase, though, was mostly due to trade-ups of existing homeowners rather than new buyers, as opposed to appreciation in home prices.
"More trade-up buyers are out," Tuccillo said. "This reflects the fact the economy is driving this."
